strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-motivated, with a clean two-stage framing (draft experts + verdict synthesizer) that directly targets error propagation in information-intensive VQA.

Empirical evaluation is broad and thorough: four benchmarks, two verdict models (GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-VL-72B), multiple ablations (number of experts, selection strategy, selection criteria, verdict input, verdict scale, model pool compositions), cost analysis, and qualitative recovery analysis.

The recovery/correction analysis (Figure 4, Table 6) is a nice contribution beyond headline accuracy, quantifying SV's ability to recover minority-correct and even zero-correct cases, and the error analysis of the tool-driven DeepEyes baseline (Appendix F) is informative.
The consensus scoring mechanism is training-free, plug-and-play, and computed cheaply via prefill NLL, with normalization against each peer's own answer to handle calibration differences.
Reproducibility support is good: code release, detailed configurations, prompt templates, and dataset statistics are provided.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially a multi-model ensemble (NLL-based answer selection) followed by synthesis by a stronger model. The 'speculative decoding' inspiration is largely a metaphor—there is no draft-verify acceptance/rejection mechanism analogous to actual speculative decoding, so the framing risks overstating the novelty relative to prior LLM ensembling/aggregation work (e.g., Universal Self-Consistency, learned aggregators) that the authors themselves cite.

A key missing baseline: sampling multiple chain-of-thought paths from the verdict model itself (self-consistency or USC-style synthesis) at comparable total cost. Without this, it is unclear whether gains come from the multi-model design or simply from giving a strong model more inference-time compute and richer context.

Fairness concerns in comparisons: the verdict receives an additional PP-StructureV3-parsed structured image input that the GPT-4o baseline does not, and the total pipeline cost (5 draft models + consensus NLL computation + verdict call) is not fully accounted against single-model baselines; only GPT-4o verdict token cost is reported (Table 5).

Some results are modest or mixed: ChartMuseum gains over the best draft expert are only 1.3%, and on HR-Bench 4K SV with GPT-4o verdict (71.4) underperforms both the best draft expert (73.0) and the 72B baseline (73.1). No statistical significance testing or variance estimates are reported anywhere.

The consensus expert selection mechanism's benefit is under-explained: as shown in Figure 3, the selected experts can include incorrect answers while higher-consensus correct answers may be deprioritized, and the ablation in Figure 6 shows best-reference only marginally trails cross-all, raising questions about how much the mechanism actually contributes versus simply forwarding several paths.

Table 3 (verdict scale ablation) is run on an arbitrary 1000-sample subset rather than the full test set, weakening the reliability of that ablation; the HR-Bench 4K evaluation is also based on only 200 questions.

The claim of 'reduced inference cost for the large verdict model' is somewhat contradictory: the verdict still processes thousands of prefill tokens from three reasoning paths plus two images, and the method does not reduce the large model's per-call cost—it merely avoids multi-turn calls, which should be quantified against the relevant iterative baselines.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with a well-motivated problem setting (information-intensive VQA) and a clean two-stage draft-then-verdict design.

Comprehensive ablation studies covering the number of draft experts, consensus selection strategies, verdict textual input, verdict scale, model pool compositions (7-9B and 2-4B pools), and visual/structured input configurations.

Evaluation spans multiple relevant benchmarks (InfographicVQA, ChartMuseum, ChartQAPro, HR-Bench 4K), and the error/recovery analysis (Figure 4, Appendix C) provides insight into the minority-correct failure mode.
Training-free nature, released code, cost analysis of the verdict stage (Appendix B), and detailed prompt templates in the appendix support reproducibility.
The analysis of DeepEyes' failure modes (Appendix F) is a useful contribution to understanding why tool-driven zoom pipelines struggle on dense layouts.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially multi-model ensembling with an LLM-as-judge/synthesizer applied to VQA. The connection to speculative decoding is largely metaphorical — there is no draft-verify token-level mechanism, no rejection sampling, and no formal guarantee; renaming ensembling as 'drafting' and synthesis as 'verdict' does not constitute a technical contribution. It closely parallels Universal Self-Consistency and rationale-aggregation work the authors themselves cite.

Missing critical baseline: GPT-4o (the verdict model) with self-consistency or its own multi-path synthesis is never compared. Since the verdict performs all the synthesis, a natural and important question is whether simply sampling multiple reasoning paths from the strong verdict model achieves the same gains — this omission weakens the central cost-efficiency and error-correction claims.

The consensus score is ad hoc and of questionable validity: NLL of a candidate answer is heavily sensitive to surface form (e.g., '49%' vs '49 percent') and model calibration; the |NLL(yi)−NLL(yj)| normalization is heuristic and no analysis of when/why it identifies reliable experts is provided beyond aggregate accuracy.

The zero-correct recovery claims (2.5-4.5% of cases where neither drafts nor verdict are individually correct) actually undermine the error-correction narrative: recovering answers no model can produce suggests the verdict is exploiting parametric knowledge or lucky guessing rather than 'synthesizing decomposable evidence,' and this alternative explanation is not analyzed.

Evaluation weaknesses: HR-Bench 4K has only 200 questions, so the reported 1-3% differences (71.4 vs 73.0 vs 75.6) are a handful of samples; no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported anywhere, despite many claimed gains of 1-4%.

Internal inconsistencies in reported numbers undermine confidence: Table 1 reports Qwen2.5-VL-72B at 84.2 while Table 7 reports 84.4 for the same configuration; Table 3 reports GPT-4o verdict at 89.4 on a 1000-sample subset while Table 2/Table 1 report 88.4; the 'Verdict w/o input' rows differ across Tables 9 and 10 (85.9 vs 88.3 on InfographicVQA) with unclear configuration distinctions.

Incomplete cost accounting: the cost analysis covers only the GPT-4o verdict call; the draft stage requires 5 VLM inferences plus k×(k−1) NLL prefill computations per question, which is substantial overhead that is not quantified or compared against simply running a strong model directly.

The consensus expert selection is evaluated against only a 'divergence' variant and 'best-reference'; comparing against simple baselines (e.g., always selecting the same top-k strongest models, or random selection) is missing, leaving the contribution of the NLL-based selection mechanism under-evidenced.

strengths: The proposed Speculative Verdict (SV) framework is well-motivated and clearly presented: using lightweight draft VLMs to generate diverse reasoning paths and a single strong verdict model call to synthesize them is a sensible, training-free design that directly targets error propagation in information-intensive VQA.

The consensus expert selection mechanism (pairwise NLL-based agreement scoring with calibration against each peer's own answer) is a clean, plug-and-play contribution that is cheap to compute via prefill only.

The evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: four benchmarks spanning information-intensive and high-resolution settings, comparisons against closed-source, open-source, and tool-driven (DeepEyes) baselines, and extensive ablations (number of experts m, selection strategy and criterion, verdict input modality, verdict scale, majority voting vs. verdict, and multiple draft pool compositions including 2-4B pools).

The error-correction analysis (Figures 4, 9; Table 6) is insightful, isolating minority-correct and zero-correct cases and quantifying when SV exceeds simple answer aggregation, with qualitative examples supporting the mechanism.
Cost accounting for the verdict call and a reproducibility statement with full prompt templates strengthen transparency and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The connection to speculative decoding is largely metaphorical: there is no token-level verification, rejection sampling, or distributional consistency with a target model. In substance the method is closer to multi-model ensembling with an LLM-as-judge synthesizer, which reduces the framing's novelty relative to prior work on universal self-consistency and learned aggregators (which are discussed but not empirically compared).

Novelty of the overall recipe is moderate; each component (CoT drafts, NLL-based agreement, LLM synthesis of rationales) exists in prior literature, and the main contribution is their combination in the multimodal domain.

The cost-efficiency claim is not fully substantiated: Table 5 reports only the verdict-call cost, excluding the expense of running five draft VLMs (two of which are 'thinking' models). A full end-to-end cost/latency comparison against GPT-4o alone, Qwen2.5-VL-72B alone, and self-consistency sampling is needed to support the efficiency narrative.

Gains over the strongest single draft expert are modest on some benchmarks (e.g., +1.3% on ChartMuseum), and much of the reported improvement depends on GPT-4o as verdict; results with the open-source Qwen-72B verdict are notably weaker and lack statistical significance analysis (no error bars or multiple-run variance for any results).
HR-Bench 4K contains only 200 questions, making the +2.5% margin over the verdict model on that benchmark statistically fragile.

Missing baselines for the aggregation component: multimodal instantiations of universal self-consistency or rationale-synthesis aggregators under identical draft paths would more precisely isolate the benefit of the verdict stage versus existing aggregation methods.

strengths: Clear and practical training-free framework: the draft-then-verdict decomposition is well-motivated for information-intensive VQA, where zoom-based tool pipelines struggle with dispersed evidence, and the paper convincingly identifies the minority-correct failure mode of majority voting that its synthesis-based verdict addresses.

Comprehensive evaluation across six benchmarks (InfographicVQA, ChartMuseum, ChartQAPro, HR-Bench 4K, TallyQA, MathVista) with a broad baseline set including proprietary models, strong open-source VLMs, RL-trained tool-driven methods (DeepEyes, Pixel-Reasoner), and LMM-as-a-Judge baselines (LLaVA-Critic), with results reproduced by the authors rather than copied from papers.

Extensive and genuinely informative ablations: number of experts m, selection strategies (cross-all vs. best-reference vs. divergence), consensus normalization (with selection-collapse analysis), NLL estimation strategy, verdict scale, textual input ablations (reasoning paths vs. answers only), visual input to the verdict, and draft pool compositions including much smaller 2-4B pools.

Good analysis depth: recovery statistics conditioned on verdict correctness, expert-combination analysis for minority-correct cases, failure mode analysis of both SV and the tool-driven baseline, and cost/token-efficiency comparisons against GPT-4o and o1.
The consensus-based expert selection via peer NLL agreement is a simple but effective plug-and-play contribution, well supported by the normalization and off-policy ablations in the appendix.
The paper is clearly written, with the method (Sections 3.2-3.4) precisely specified and prompt templates fully provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially answer-level ensembling with NLL-based peer consensus plus LLM-as-a-judge synthesis. The 'speculative decoding' framing is largely an analogy — there is no actual draft-verify token-level mechanism, rejection sampling, or correctness guarantee — and the closest prior art (multi-draft collaborative decoding, DivCon, learned aggregation methods) is only qualitatively distinguished.

Heavy dependence on the verdict model: the largest gains come from GPT-4o as verdict (+11.9 ANLS on InfographicVQA), and the开源 verdict variant gains are much smaller (84.0/44.1/59.0 vs. baselines). It is not fully clear how much of the improvement is the framework versus simply feeding GPT-4o richer textual context; the verdict ablations partially address but do not fully resolve this concern.

Cost-efficiency claims require scrutiny: Table 6 reports SV is ~2-3x more expensive than GPT-4o alone per sample, so the efficiency argument holds only relative to o1; the compute cost of the 5-model draft stage plus k x (k-1) NLL scoring forward passes (including image prefill for scoring) is not transparently itemized, so the 'minimizing computational cost' claim is somewhat overstated.

Some results show the structured PP-StructureV3 auxiliary input yields negligible or even negative gains (Table 22), raising questions about the auxiliary-input configuration and why it is kept in the main setup; also a few inconsistencies (e.g., Table 21 vs. 22 'w/o input' rows) could confuse readers.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting (e.g., over random 1000-sample subsets in Table 5), and gains on some benchmarks (ChartMuseum +1.3 over best draft) are within plausible run-to-run noise.

Potential confound in baseline fairness: baselines are evaluated with CoT prompting but apparently without the structured image auxiliary input, and per-benchmark prompt customization (official templates adapted per dataset) introduces some tuning asymmetry that is disclosed but not fully controlled.
Reproducibility partially depends on a proprietary verdict model (GPT-4o), and the anonymized code is in supplementary material rather than a public release.

strengths: Extensive and well-organized empirical evaluation across six benchmarks (InfographicVQA, ChartMuseum, ChartQAPro, HR-Bench 4K, TallyQA, MathVista), including fair-to-thorough baselines covering closed-source, open-source, and tool-driven methods

Comprehensive ablation studies: number of draft experts, consensus vs. best-reference vs. divergence selection, verdict input format, verdict scale, normalization effects, and NLL estimation strategy — this is well above the average level of ablation rigor

Useful error analysis: recovery breakdown by expert-correctness categories, per-model complementarity analysis (Appendix I), failure mode analysis for both SV and tool-driven baselines (Appendices I–K), and cost/token analysis

The consensus-based expert selection via normalized pairwise NLL is a reasonable, plug-and-play mechanism, and the analysis of calibration-induced selection collapse (Appendix F) is a genuinely interesting empirical finding
Training-free approach with demonstrated gains over the verdict model itself (e.g., +11.9 on InfographicVQA over GPT-4o) and on par or better than o1 at 15–26% of its API cost
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core mechanism is essentially an ensemble of CoT generations followed by LLM-as-a-judge synthesis, which is closely related to self-consistency, Universal Self-Consistency, LLaVA-Critic, and multi-model collaboration methods the authors themselves cite (e.g., SpecReason, Speculative Thinking). The 'speculative decoding' framing is largely superficial — there is no draft-verify mechanism, no rejection sampling, and no theoretical connection to the speculative decoding literature; the verdict does not 'verify' drafts in any analogous sense

Fairness concerns in headline comparisons: the verdict model receives an auxiliary PP-StructureV3 layout-annotated image that the GPT-4o/Qwen baselines in Table 1 do not appear to receive, so some of the reported gains over the raw verdict baseline may stem from the enriched input rather than the framework (Table 22 partially addresses this but leaves ambiguity about the exact baseline configuration)

Cost-efficiency claims are based only on API token costs; running five separate draft VLMs per question plus a large verdict is a substantial total compute burden that is not fully accounted for, making the 'minimizing computational cost' claim weaker than presented

Some reported results undercut the headline claims: on HR-Bench 4K with GPT-4o as verdict (71.4), SV underperforms the 7B Qwen2.5-VL draft expert (73.0) and DeepEyes (73.0), so 'SV surpasses all baselines' holds only under the alternative verdict configuration; no statistical significance or variance estimates are reported for any comparison

The method's benefit depends heavily on the verdict model's quality (Table 4 shows small verdicts provide negligible gains), meaning the contribution reduces in practice to 'give a strong model extra candidates and ask it to synthesize' — a relatively incremental insight despite the elaborate framing

Consensus-based selection may systematically exclude the minority-correct experts that the paper claims to rescue, creating tension between the selection mechanism (favoring agreement) and the error-correction narrative (favoring minority views); the paper does not quantify how often the mechanism filters out exactly the correct minority drafts

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and increasingly important problem: information-intensive visual reasoning over charts, infographics, and high-resolution images, where localization and multi-hop evidence integration are error-sensitive.

The proposed Speculative Verdict framework is training-free, plug-and-play, and clearly described: multiple lightweight draft VLMs generate CoT reasoning paths, a consensus-based NLL score selects the most agreed-upon experts, and a large verdict model synthesizes the paths in a single prefill-dominated call.

The empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive: four main benchmarks plus TallyQA and MathVista for generalization; comparisons against closed-source (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o1), open-source (including 72B verdict-scale models), and tool-driven RL baselines (DeepEyes, Pixel-Reasoner); results with two different verdict models (GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-VL-72B) to show the gains are not verdict-specific.

Ablations are thorough and cover all design choices: number of draft experts (m), selection strategy (cross-all vs. best-reference vs. divergence), consensus normalization and NLL estimation strategy (Appendix F), verdict scale (Table 4), verdict input configuration including visual and structured OCR inputs (Appendix H), and prompt templates (Appendix M).

The error-correction analysis (Figure 4, Tables 10-11, Appendix I) is a genuine strength: the 47-53% recovery of minority-correct cases and even some zero-correct recoveries (with qualitative example in Appendix L) demonstrate that SV is more than simple majority voting, which is directly validated against majority voting and LLaVA-Critic judge baselines.

Cost-efficiency analysis (Tables 5-6, 8-9, 18) is careful and quantitative, showing SV outperforms GPT-4o/o1 at 15-26% of o1's cost, and includes per-benchmark token counts and failure-mode analysis of both SV (Appendix J) and the tool-driven baseline (Appendix K).

Model-pool ablations (Appendix E) show robustness across model scales (2-4B, 7-9B, reasoning and non-reasoning pools), and supplementary material includes anonymized code and full prompts, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate. The method is essentially a heterogeneous ensemble with an NLL-based consensus filter and a strong model as synthesizer. The speculative decoding framing, while rhetorically appealing, is loose: there is no token/step-level verification, acceptance/rejection criterion, or distributional guarantee connecting the method to speculative decoding beyond the loose draft-then-verify analogy, and the paper acknowledges existing speculative-reasoning work (SpecReason, speculative thinking) without clearly differentiating its technical mechanism from LMM-as-a-judge and synthesis ensembling.

Potential evaluation fairness concern: GPT-4o baseline results may not benefit from the PP-StructureV3 structured image input that SV's verdict receives (Section 4.1), so part of the reported +11.9% gain over GPT-4o could come from the enriched input rather than the framework. Table 22 shows structured input adds little on top of SV, but a GPT-4o-with-structured-input baseline is not reported.

The verdict input length ablation (Table 3) and token analysis (Tables 18) show SV consumes substantial prefill tokens (700-3100+ per sample); while costs are reported, latency analysis is missing, and prefill cost dominates the reported $/sample only for API pricing, not for self-hosted deployment.

Gains on some benchmarks are modest relative to the added system complexity (e.g., +2.5% over the 72B verdict on InfographicVQA, +1.3-2.6% over the best draft expert on several benchmarks), and ChartMuseum gains with GPT-4o verdict (49.3) are below o1's 50.6 on the sampled subset (Table 5), slightly tempering the 'outperforms proprietary models' claim.

The consensus score assumes a single unique correct answer, which may not hold for open-ended questions; behavior on such questions is not analyzed, and InfographicVQA's ANLS metric partially handles format mismatch whereas ChartMuseum/ChartQAPro accuracy metrics could interact differently with answer-style consensus.

Several important analyses (selection frequency, normalization, LLaVA-Critic comparison details) are deferred to appendices; the main text could better quantify the consensus-selection accuracy (e.g., how often the selected experts actually contain the correct answer).
